title: Explore and process multiple event types with Schema-aware Fabric Eventstreams (Preview)
text: Real-time streams rarely contain just one kind of event. A building operations stream, for example, might carry thermostat readings, occupancy updates, air-quality measurements, and badge-reader activity through the same source. These events may share a payload format, but they don't describe the same thing. A temperature field matters to a thermostat event. An employee identifier belongs to an access event. An occupancy count describes something else entirely. Traditionally, processing a mixed stream like this often meant treating it as one wide, sparse schema or reconstructing the meaning of each event downstream. Developers identify the event type, guard against fields that don't apply, and often repeat that logic wherever the stream branches. With Schema-aware Fabric Eventstreams (Preview) , Eventstreams can preserve and use the shape of an event while the data is still in motion . You can explore individual event shapes, distinguish multiple event types within the same stream, and build processing logic against the event type you need. This works with events that reference registered schemas, events organized through classification, and untyped events whose structure is not yet defined. For developers working with mixed streams, this means building logic around each event type instead of repeatedly reconstructing its identity downstream. The event’s identity and shape become part of the streaming workflow, not just something to interpret after the data lands. Explore the events arriving in your stream When several event types share a feed, looking at the union of every field only tells part of the story. The schema-aware data preview feature organizes streaming data by event type, so you can focus on the shape you want to understand. For a thermostat event, you can inspect the fields describing temperature, humidity, location, and device state. Switch to an occupancy event, and the preview reflects fields for counts, zones, and observation time. To understand an unfamiliar event before configuring processing logic, inspect its payload, headers, and metadata, expand nested JSON, and open its individual details. Export selected data when you need to examine representative events further. More importantly, you can understand those differences while the stream is live , before building processing logic or waiting for the data to land somewhere else. Figure: Schema-aware data preview groups events with registered schemas (schematized events), classified events, and untyped events. Work with schemas at different levels of maturity Not every event producer is at the same point in its schema journey. Some applications publish against established, versioned contracts (schemas). Others already carry useful type information such as deviceType or eventType, but don’t have registered schemas. Still others produce events that are new, evolving, or not yet fully documented. Schema-aware Eventstreams lets those different events coexist in the same Eventstream through registered, classified, and untyped events. Schematized events: reuse established contracts For producers with defined contracts, schema-aware Eventstreams (Preview) can use schemas managed through Event SchemaSet, which is generally available, and Fabric’s Schema Registry. Events that reference these registered schemas are called schematized events. They use the CloudEvents format, with the ce_type header identifying the registered event type so Eventstreams can use the corresponding schema for exploration and processing. This gives producers and consumers an explicit, reusable definition of the event rather than deriving its meaning from whichever fields happen to appear in a sample. See how registered schemas work in Eventstreams . Classified events: find structure in existing streams Many useful streams don't start with registered contracts. A mixed JSON feed may already contain fields such as deviceType, eventType, or entityType that identify what each event represents. In the new Classifier workflow, select that field to organize the stream into distinct event types. In our building example, deviceType can separate thermostat, occupancy, air-quality, and badge-reader events even though they continue through the same Eventstream. Classification doesn't turn those events into registered contracts. It makes their existing structure usable for exploration and processing. Figure: The deviceType classifier separates a mixed stream into four event types with distinct detected fields. Untyped events: keep the unknown visible An event can still be inspected even when it has neither a registered schema nor a user-selected classifier. Untyped events keep that traffic visible without requiring you to define its structure first. Events from sources that aren’t associated with an Event SchemaSet can remain untyped or be organized through classification. In classified streams, events with a missing or null classifier value remain untyped. Events from schema-associated sources that fail validation are dropped and reported in runtime logs, not routed as untyped. This gives you room to inspect new or unmatched traffic and decide later whether it should be classified, registered, or continue as untyped. Build against each event, not the entire stream Seeing the different shapes is useful. Using those shapes while processing the stream is where schema awareness becomes especially powerful. Supported operators and destinations can select a registered, classified, or untyped event as their input. The fields available for configuration then correspond to that event shape rather than every field observed across the source. Suppose you want to identify high-temperature readings. That logic belongs to thermostat events. It shouldn't need to account for occupancy counts, badge identifiers, or air-quality attributes just because those events happen to travel through the same stream. For example, select the thermostat event as the input to the Filter operator and use its temperature field to identify high-temperature readings. That branch can focus on thermostat data, while occupancy, air-quality, and badge-reader events continue through the same Eventstream and follow their own processing paths. The same model extends to supported destinations such as Eventhouse, Lakehouse, custom endpoints, and derived streams. A destination can consume the selected event shape instead of treating a heterogeneous source as one undifferentiated feed. Figure: The Input schema list makes individual shapes available to the Filter operator. This shifts an important responsibility upstream. Instead of repeatedly reconstructing event type in downstream queries, applications, or transformations, the Eventstream itself can carry that processing context while the data is moving. Start where your data is today Adopting schemas doesn’t have to be the mandatory first step. Different producers have different owners, technologies, release schedules, and contract maturity. Requiring every producer to register a schema before you can distinguish event shapes can delay the value you expect from stream processing. Schema-aware Eventstreams lets you take a progressive approach: Register stable contracts that teams want to discover and reuse. Classify existing mixed feeds that already contain a meaningful type signal. Keep untyped traffic visible when its shape isn't known yet. Move toward registered contracts where stronger schema governance provides value. One Eventstream can therefore work with several event types and levels of schema maturity without forcing every producer to change at the same time. Start with the data you have today and introduce stronger contracts where they make sense. Schema-aware Eventstreams brings the meaning of an event into the streaming workflow itself. title: Create purpose-built custom visuals in Real-Time Dashboards with Copilot (Preview)
text: Real-Time Dashboards include built-in visuals for common monitoring and analysis scenarios. However, operational decisions do not always fit a standard chart. You may need to combine several signals, use a domain-specific layout, or present information differently for a particular workflow or audience. Custom visuals with Copilot, now in preview, help you create a dashboard experience around the operational question you need to answer. With custom visuals, you can describe the operational view you need in natural language. Copilot creates the supporting KQL query and HTML-based visualization directly in the dashboard, helping you move from an operational question to a tailored visual without first adapting the scenario to a predefined chart. Move beyond predefined chart types A standard chart starts with a visual type such as a line, bar, or pie chart. You then shape the query and formatting to fit that structure. This model works well when the question maps naturally to an established chart. Operational questions don't always fit that model. You might need a visual that combines several signals, uses a domain-specific layout, or presents status in a form that matches how your team works. Building that experience outside the dashboard can require front-end development and separate deployment and maintenance processes. Custom visuals begin with the outcome instead. Describe the operational question and the visual you want, and Copilot uses the selected database context to generate both the KQL query and an HTML-based visualization. The result is added directly to the dashboard as a new tile. Example: Turn venue metrics into an operational view Consider a venue operations dashboard that tracks wait times and ingress volume across several entrances. Standard KPI and chart visuals can show those measures individually, but an operator may need to understand how conditions differ across the venue. With a custom visual, the dashboard author can describe that operational view directly: arrange entrances spatially around the venue, show the current wait time and ingress volume for each entrance, and use color to highlight congestion. Copilot can then generate a visual design around that scenario. The result is not simply another way to plot the same data. It presents the information in a form designed around the operational question: Where is congestion building, and which entrance needs attention? Create a custom visual Start from a Real-Time Dashboard that you can edit, and that has its data sources to create a custom visual, open a Real-Time Dashboard that you can edit and confirm that its data sources are configured for custom visuals. In Editing mode, select Add visual > Describe a visual, enter your prompt, and submit it. Copilot adds the visual to the current dashboard page and generates the connected KQL query and HTML-based visualization Figure: In Editing mode, select Add visual, and then select Describe a visual to begin creating a custom visual. Figure: Copilot displays a generated KQL query and the connected custom visual in the dashboard. Review the first result as a starting point. The quality of the visual depends in part on how clearly the prompt communicates the question, the data to use, and the intended presentation. Figure: Review the generated entrance operations visual. Write a focused prompt A useful prompt gives Copilot enough context to choose the relevant data and design a visual that answers a specific question. Include the following details: The operational question: Explain the decision or condition that the visual should support. Measures: Name the values to calculate or compare, such as event count, latency, volume, or service state. Dimensions: Identify how to group or organize the results, such as location, service, category, or severity. Time range: Define the period that matters, such as the last hour or the last 24 hours. Presentation: Describe the visual form when you have a specific operational layout in mind. Interactions: Describe how viewers should explore the visual, such as displaying additional details or using controls to change what is shown. For example, you can ask Copilot to: Show the current operational status of each venue entrance. Display average wait time and ingress volume for each entrance and use color to make congestion immediately visible. Arrange the entrances spatially around the venue so operators can quickly identify where attention is needed. Create a storm monitoring view that positions storm events by latitude and longitude. Size each event based on severity and use color to distinguish warning levels. Show additional event details when a viewer explores an event. Create a service health board that shows each service and its dependencies as connected nodes. Use color to distinguish healthy, degraded, and critical services, and make critical services visually prominent so operators can quickly identify where investigation is needed. These prompts do more than name a chart. They describe the relationship between the data and the way a viewer should interpret it. You can make them more precise by adding the relevant measures, status rules, categories, or time window from your data. Review and refine the result Creating a custom visual is an iterative authoring experience. After Copilot creates the tile, review whether the visual answers the intended question and whether the generated query selects and aggregates the expected data. To make changes, select the Edit icon on the tile. In tile edit mode, you can review the query and the visual, then use the Copilot pane to refine either one. Follow-up prompts can clarify the original request without requiring you to start over. For example, you might narrow the time range, change the grouping, emphasize a service state, or adjust how the information is presented. Continue until the visual communicates the operational state clearly. Then select Apply , resize, or reposition the tile, and save the dashboard. Switch to viewing mode to confirm that the saved visual renders as expected in the experience your dashboard viewers use. This review step is important for AI-assisted authoring. Validate the generated query and visuals against your data and operational requirements. Clear labels, appropriate aggregation, and a focused visual hierarchy help viewers understand the result quickly. Next steps Start with an operational question that does not fit a standard chart. Describe the experience you need and use Copilot to create a first version that you can review and refine before sharing the dashboard. This approach helps you turn specialized monitoring needs into tailored operational views without building and maintaining a separate front-end experience. Learn how to configure the required identity and cloud connection, create a tile, write a focused prompt, and refine the result in Create a custom visual in a Real-Time Dashboard . Explore the built-in options in the Real-Time Dashboard visual gallery . Review formatting options for standard tiles in Customize Real-Time Dashboard visuals .

title: Incrementally migrate and re-migrate database objects with Migration Assistant for Fabric Warehouse (Preview)
text: Migrate database objects to Microsoft Fabric in phases without creating a new Warehouse for every run. Start with one business domain, add another when it is ready, or revisit an object after its source definition changes. You can also build on an existing Warehouse instead of replacing it. Incremental migration for Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview) lets you move workloads in manageable phases while keeping control of the destination. Select the objects required for the current workload, add more objects in later runs, and resolve naming conflicts when an incoming object already exists. The process migrates object definitions; it does not continuously synchronize changed rows. You can start with an empty Warehouse, continue a previous migration, or use an existing Warehouse that was not created through migration. This flexibility lets teams preserve completed work while adding the next approved scope. It also supports deliberate consolidation into the Fabric destinations that match your architecture. Choose the objects that belong in each migration Enterprise migration plans often span several teams, applications, and business domains. Those groups do not always need to move together. Incremental migration lets you define the scope of each run. Instead of including every source object, select the objects needed for the workload you are moving. For example, start with the schemas, tables, and views required by one business domain. Review the translated definitions and validate the dependent workload before expanding the scope. In a later run, return to the same Warehouse and add the next approved set of objects. In the destination Warehouse, open the Migration tab and select Get more objects . Provide the source connection or upload a supported source input, and then select Choose more objects to migrate to define the next set. Figure: Use Get more objects to start another migration run from the destination Warehouse. Figure: Select source objects and review dependencies and naming conflicts before migration. Before you start the run, review the complete object list populated in the selection dialog. The list flags naming conflicts and adds direct dependencies for selected objects. Confirm that every included object is necessary for the workload you intend to migrate. Filter source objects to show all objects, objects with naming conflicts, or objects without naming conflicts. Identify objects whose names already exist in the destination through warning indicators. Review each selected object’s direct dependencies before you start the migration. Migration Assistant includes those dependencies by default, so the final scope can contain more objects than you initially selected. Review the source, destination, selected objects, and included dependencies in the summary. Confirm that every object belongs in the current scope and that naming conflicts have an owner. The Migration Assistant guide for connecting to a source system describes the workflow. Build on an empty or existing warehouse The destination does not have to come from an earlier migration or a specific migration mode. Choose the destination based on the workload, ownership model, security boundary, and naming plan. The following starting points are supported. An empty Warehouse: Begin with a destination you have prepared and migrate the first set of objects into it. A previously migrated Warehouse: Add more objects or revisit selected objects from an earlier run. A Warehouse that was not created through migration: Bring source objects into a Warehouse that already contains work created through other means. You do not need to create another Warehouse just because you are starting another migration run. Reusing a destination can reduce unnecessary duplication and keep related objects together. Confirm, however, that the shared destination fits the workload and data-isolation requirements. Re-migrate objects with control Migration work often requires revisiting an earlier decision. A source definition can change after the first run, or a translated object might need correction after validation. Re-migration lets you return to that object without treating the entire source as a new migration. When an incoming object's name already exists in the destination, Migration Assistant identifies a naming conflict. Objects without naming conflicts can be created immediately. Conflicting objects remain pending and are not created or replaced until you explicitly choose how to resolve each conflict. For each conflict, compare the SQL definitions side by side: the existing definition on the left and the incoming translated definition on the right. Review the full definition, not only the highlighted difference, because connected changes can affect downstream objects. Then choose the action that fits the object. Keep existing: Retain the destination's current definition and discard the incoming translated definition. Keep incoming: Replace the existing definition with the incoming translated definition, confirming the action when prompted. Rename incoming: Create the incoming object under a different name while retaining the existing object. Conflict handling makes re-migration an explicit decision. You can preserve work already completed in Fabric, accept a revised source definition, or keep both definitions under different names. Record the chosen action so that workload owners understand which definition is active. Figure: Compare existing and incoming definitions before resolving a naming conflict. Replacing an object changes its definition in the destination and may require you to reload data or revalidate dependent workloads. Before you replace a table, view, or procedure, identify the objects and processes that use it and plan the required follow-up work. For detailed behavior, refer to Resolve conflicts and fix objects . Consolidate your data estate Incremental migration lets you move selected objects from supported SQL Server databases, Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pools, or Teradata databases into one or more Fabric Warehouses. A separate destination Warehouse is not required for every source database or migration run. The destination design should still reflect workload ownership, security, naming, and data-isolation requirements. This approach supports several consolidation patterns. Choose a pattern only after confirming that the workloads can share the same operational and security boundaries. Common uses are listed below. Consolidate objects from multiple databases on the same source platform. Bring together selected objects from different supported source platforms. Expand the same Warehouse as additional databases and workloads are ready to migrate. As you add objects, conflict handling helps you manage names already present in the destination. Compare existing and incoming definitions, then keep the existing object, replace it with the incoming definition, or rename the incoming object. This decision determines which definition becomes part of the consolidated Warehouse. Consolidating destinations does not automatically reconcile definitions or combine table data. Review dependencies, naming conventions, permissions, ownership, and data-loading requirements before each run. These checks help the consolidated Warehouse reflect the intended architecture rather than an accidental collection of objects. Keep object migration and data loading distinct In this preview, incremental migration means selecting, adding, or revisiting database object definitions across separate migration runs. It covers object selection, translation, dependency handling, and definition conflicts, but it does not continuously synchronize changed rows. After migrating the required definitions and resolving conflicts, plan the associated data movement. title: Microsoft & Snowflake’s Commitment to Apache Ossie
text: If you haven't already, check out FabCon and SQLCon 2026 in Barcelona: Building the data foundation for Microsoft Copilot and Agents for a complete look at all of our FabCon Europe announcements across Fabric and Microsoft Databases. Advancing an open, interoperable semantic foundation for AI-powered analytics Today, Microsoft is pleased to affirm our commitment to Apache Ossie (incubating) , a community-led effort to establish a vendor-neutral standard for exchanging semantic metadata across analytics, AI, and BI platforms. This has been a close collaboration with Snowflake, who helped found Ossie . We have heard loud and clear that customers want to enable platform-agnostic agentic experiences. Shared semantic context must be defined once and reused across platforms, enabling agentic consumption at scale, maximizing the reach of AI-powered analytics, and empowering users to leverage the best agent for the job. Power BI semantic models are key enablers of AI-powered analysis, providing humans and AI agents with governed semantic context to answer data questions quickly and confidently. Power BI semantic models have more than 38 million monthly active users and are adopted by 94% of Fortune 500 companies. Microsoft was also recognized as a Leader and Outperformer in the GigaOm’s radar for semantic layers & metric stores in 2025. We’re now bringing this wealth of experience to Apache Ossie, and we are excited to work with Snowflake and other partners to help make the project successful. Why Apache Ossie matters Until now, semantic definitions were often recreated across platforms, introducing complexity, inconsistency, and management overhead. Apache Ossie addresses this with a common specification that tools can read and write. Its goal is straightforward but consequential: define a semantic layer once and make it portable across the data and AI ecosystem, while preserving semantic meaning and governance for agentic consumption. Collaboration with Snowflake Snowflake and Microsoft serve many of the same customers, but customers don't want to choose between ecosystems. They want their data and analytics investments to work together. That makes interoperability between, for example, Snowflake Semantic Views and Power BI semantic models a shared responsibility. This layers on top of the integration work we have already done with Snowflake for writing Iceberg tables from Snowflake to OneLake , Mirrored Databases from Snowflake , using Iceberg tables with OneLake , Catalog Integration for OneLake , Power Query Snowflake connector and much more. As discussed in the Snowflake blog post and the message below from Carl Perry, VP of Analytics at Snowflake, our collaboration is currently focused on using Apache Ossie as a vehicle for cross-platform semantic-layer conversion without moving or duplicating the underlying data. Looking ahead, we’re committed to advancing the open standard by building on our deep expertise in semantic modeling by, including helping establish DAX as an Ossie-recognized query language. We also plan to help advance Ossie support for ontologies so customers can extend the business logic in semantic models beyond agentic analysis and into platform-agnostic operational intelligence. Ultimately our goal is simple: enable customers to define once, and reuse anywhere . Today, we are highlighting the following new integration scenario: converting an Ossie document into both a Snowflake Semantic View and a Power BI semantic model. This enables customers to define shared semantic context once, then reuse it across Snowflake and Fabric while retaining the agentic experiences and capabilities of each platform. Refer to Apache Ossie Microsoft Converter for more information. Building together We look forward to working with the Apache community, Snowflake, and others across the industry to create a more open and connected future for AI-powered analytics, delivering more choice and flexibility for customers. Get involved: Visit the Apache Ossie project website and repository to explore the specification and community contribution channels. Share your thoughts and feedback with us. Apache Ossie is undergoing incubation at the Apache Software Foundation. Incubation indicates that the project is working toward the governance, infrastructure, and community practices expected of established Apache projects.

title: Simplify Teradata migrations with Fabric Migration Assistant (Preview)
text: Migrating an enterprise Teradata estate to Microsoft Fabric can require extensive manual work across database objects, SQL and BTEQ code, dependencies, and operational processes. Fabric Migration Assistant helps reduce that effort so teams can focus their review on the objects and workflows that need attention. Fabric Migration Assistant for Data Warehouse now supports Teradata sources in preview. It converts eligible Teradata metadata and code to Fabric-compatible T-SQL, deploys eligible destination definitions, and flags scripts that need review or remediation, reducing the manual effort required to prepare a migration. You can choose which objects to migrate, review the translated code, and focus remediation on exceptions instead of manually translating every eligible object. Migration Assistant does not move the associated data; you load data in the following step of the migration flow. Define a migration scope you can validate Reduce migration risk by starting with a representative set of interdependent objects from one workload or business process. Keeping the related tables, views, procedures, functions, and macros together lets you evaluate the translated result as a working unit. A focused scope makes it easier to distinguish among three outcomes: Translation: The source definition was converted to Fabric-compatible T-SQL. Deployment: The translated definition was created successfully in the destination warehouse. Validation: The migrated workload produces the expected behavior and results. Translate Teradata metadata into Fabric-compatible T-SQL Package your Teradata .sql and .bteq files into a ZIP archive, including the object definitions and dependencies needed for the selected scope. From the Fabric workspace, open Migrate and select Teradata (Preview) under Migrate to a warehouse. The guided experience lets you upload the archive, choose the objects in scope, and confirm the destination before migration begins. Migration Assistant translates and creates eligible definitions for: Tables Views Stored procedures SQL functions Macros, which translate into stored procedures After the run, review migrated objects to see their status and translation details. This review helps you identify datatype and SQL changes that require validation before you treat successful object creation as a completed migration. Use the file-based Migration Assistant guide for the upload, object-selection, and review workflow. Focus remediation where it's needed Teradata and Fabric Data Warehouse don't have a one-to-one mapping for every construct. Some definitions translate directly; others need a different implementation. Teradata macros translate into stored procedures, while volatile tables map to local temporary tables. Review the maintained Teradata SQL translation reference for object mappings, data types, BTEQ behavior, and constructs that need redesign. Migration Assistant groups scripts that could not be translated or deployed under Objects to fix. For each object, the source definition, translation comments, and error details help you determine whether the issue requires a syntax correction or a broader change to workload behavior. If Copilot is available and enabled in your environment, Fix query errors can suggest a correction. Treat the suggestion as a starting point: compare it with the source definition and error details, revise it as needed, and run the script to validate the result before creating the object. Before accepting a corrected object, confirm that it preserves the intended workload behavior by comparing parameters, joins, filters, and transaction boundaries with the source logic. Bring BTEQ business logic into Fabric workflows BTEQ scripts can combine SQL with control flow, session management, imports, exports, and operational logic. Migrating those scripts requires attention to the surrounding workflow, not just the SQL statements. Migration Assistant translated eligible SQL and supported BTEQ elements into stored procedures. Review the generated procedures, then rebuild imports, exports, orchestration, and external operations with the appropriate Fabric capabilities. Different parts of a BTEQ workload can use different Fabric capabilities: SQL and supported control flow: Review the translated stored procedure. Data imports and exports: Use the appropriate loading or export capability, including COPY INTO or pipeline copy activities. Scheduling, orchestration, and external operations: Recreate the required behavior through Fabric pipelines or other appropriate execution environments. Translation doesn't automatically reproduce the entire operational environment. Validate parameters, error paths, sequencing, and external dependencies alongside the translated SQL. The objective is to preserve the business behavior you need while choosing suitable Fabric implementations. Figure: Animated GIF —Migration Assistant for Teradata migration showcasing metadata translation flow. Choose how to move the data Metadata migration establishes the destination definitions in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse. Data movement loads the associated rows after the required table definitions are in place. Choose the method that fits each workload: Copy job: Use the guided transfer from Migration Assistant's Copy data step. Connect to Teradata, select tables, review mappings, and choose the copy mode. A full copy can establish the initial dataset; incremental copies are an option when the source configuration supports them. Staged files and COPY INTO: For large historical transfers, unload Teradata data to Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 and load the staged files into Fabric Data Warehouse with COPY INTO. Fabric pipelines: Use pipelines when the migration needs multi-step orchestration, transformations, branching, or custom recovery logic. To learn more, refer to Migration methods for Teradata to Fabric Data Warehouse for data movement options and guidance on replacing Teradata loading utilities. Validate the migrated workload Run representative queries and compare the results with the Teradata workload. Validate row counts, aggregates, filters, joins, null handling, and the date and numeric behavior that affects the business process - not merely whether each object exists in the destination. Include both expected paths and failure paths in the test scope. For procedures and translated BTEQ logic, verify parameter handling, transaction boundaries, retry behavior, and the sequence of dependent operations. Next steps Use Plan a migration from Teradata to Fabric Data Warehouse to define the scope and validation approach. Review Translate Teradata SQL for Fabric Data Warehouse for object mappings and use Migration methods for Teradata to Fabric Data Warehouse to choose the data-movement method.

title: Connect coding agents to Fabric notebooks with FNTK (Preview)
text: The Fabric Notebook Toolkit (Preview) helps developers shorten the feedback loop between writing code and validating it with live notebook results. It connects coding agents to Microsoft Fabric notebooks through a command-line interface (CLI) that runs in the terminal alongside tools such as Claude Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Codex. An agent can inspect the current code, run one cell, review its output, make a targeted change, and run it again without resubmitting the entire notebook—much as a human programmer working interactively. Figure: Animated GIF A coding agent uses FNTK from the terminal to interact with a Microsoft Fabric notebook. From code suggestions to notebook execution A coding agent can help write a transformation, but a proposed change is not the same as a working result. When execution happens elsewhere, developers must move code into a notebook, run it, and bring the results or errors back to the agent. FNTK connects those steps so the agent can work with a running Fabric notebook and its execution results instead of relying only on code shared in the conversation. Interactive development and debugging are the central use cases. You can ask an agent to inspect a notebook, investigate a failing transformation, or validate a change using actual execution output. The notebook remains in Fabric and uses Fabric capacity for distributed data processing, while FNTK provides the terminal commands the agent uses to interact with the live session. Run, inspect, and refine one cell at a time FNTK keeps the notebook session active while the agent works, so developers can explore and refine code without repeatedly restarting the workflow. For example, an agent can inspect a schema, adjust a conversion, check several records, and return to the same transformation as new information emerges. This mirrors the iterative way developers work in notebooks and keeps each change grounded in actual execution results. The toolkit brings the operations needed for that workflow into the terminal. An agent can discover the target notebook, read and update its cells, execute code, and retrieve results. Instead of treating every adjustment as a new whole-notebook submission, it can focus on the code being investigated. Find workspaces, notebooks, and lakehouses to establish the context for the task. Read, add, or update notebook cells as the work develops. Execute a cell's code and inspect its output before deciding what to change. Reuse the live session to refine and rerun the relevant code. For example, a transformation may fail because an input column has a different type than expected. An agent can inspect the schema, revise the affected code, and rerun it in the existing session to check the result. This avoids restarting the entire notebook merely to test that change and keeps the investigation focused on the failing operation. Give the agent the evidence to debug FNTK gives the agent the execution evidence needed to determine the source of a failure. It exposes cell output and Spark job state, along with driver logs, executor logs, and logs from Livy, the service that manages Spark sessions. With this context, the agent can investigate the likely source of a problem instead of relying on source code alone. The CLI can return structured JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) responses that identify results, errors, and suggested next actions. An agent can use this information to determine whether execution has finished, retrieve diagnostics, and choose what to investigate next. This shortens the feedback loop between writing code and understanding its behavior while reducing the need to copy outputs and logs manually between tools. FNTK in practice at Microsoft For our data engineering team at Microsoft, FNTK filled a gap between generating code and working with real data. Previously, we used an AI assistant to draft code locally, then copied it into Fabric notebooks to run it and brought the results back into the conversation. With FNTK, we can stay in GitHub Copilot, execute code in Fabric, and use the results to iterate. We started by installing the toolkit, connecting with the appropriate permissions, and asking questions about a data source. Exploratory work quickly became a valuable use case. We could ask for row counts, distributions, or samples, then follow up based on the actual results. From there, we built shared workflow skills and a developer plugin around FNTK, incorporated our engineering standards, and connected the plugin to Azure DevOps through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to bring user-story context into the same workflow. In practice, this has sped up development and helped us work across multiple user stories, with more of our time spent reviewing changes rather than writing every line ourselves. Copilot handles the reasoning; FNTK provides the connection to live notebook execution. We can still inspect the runs in Fabric, and our existing source-control, quality, and human-review practices remain in place. In practice, this workflow has helped us work across multiple user stories and spend more time reviewing changes instead of writing every line ourselves. Copilot handles the reasoning; FNTK provides the connection to live notebook execution. We can still inspect the runs in Fabric, and our existing source-control, quality, and human-review practices remain in place. Figure: FNTK connects an AI developer agent to live Fabric notebook execution, alongside MCP tools for context and delivery tools for human-reviewed changes. title: From mixed events to real-time action: Fabric Eventstreams Q3 2026
text: Coauthor: Arindam Chatterjee Fabric Eventstreams makes it easy to connect to streaming sources, transform the ingested events and route them to destinations across Microsoft Fabric. But building real-time systems also requires teams to understand the events in motion, enriching them with business context, detecting and responding to any issues on time, and securely managing their streams across environments. That broader experience is the story behind this quarter’s updates. Eventstreams is expanding beyond connectivity and data movement to provide more of the capabilities teams need to work with streaming data after it arrives, while it is still in motion. With these expanded capabilities, users can now: Connect to more managed sources and extend Eventstreams with custom connectors. Capture change feeds from more operational databases. Explore and process multiple event types in a single Eventstream. Enrich streaming events with contextual data before processing and routing. Monitor processing health, diagnose problems, and act faster. Deploy with workspace-scoped networking and reusable configuration. Connect managed and custom streaming sources Eventstream added generally available managed connectors for SAP Datasphere, Cribl, Solace PubSub+, and MQTT, extending native connectivity across enterprise applications, observability pipelines, event meshes, and IoT brokers. For these common scenarios, teams can use managed connectors instead of writing and hosting connector code. Managed connectors cover a growing range of common sources. But many organizations also need to connect proprietary applications, partner products, and internal platforms. Custom Stream Connector (Preview) lets organizations bring compatible Kafka Connect source connectors into Fabric when a native connector is unavailable. Teams can manage versions, publish connectors internally or through a partner, and make them discoverable in Real-Time hub. This approach extends managed Fabric pipelines to proprietary applications, partner products, and internal platforms while allowing independent software vendors to retain control of their code and licensing. What shipped: SAP Datasphere connector (Generally Available), Cribl connector (Generally Available), Solace PubSub+ connector (Generally Available), MQTT connector (Generally Available), Custom Stream Connector (Preview). Bring operational changes into the stream Orders, inventory updates, account changes, and application state already live in operational databases. Capturing those changes is only the first step. Teams must also operate connectors, recover from failures, handle schema changes, and scale the pipeline. This complex operational work makes many CDC-based solutions difficult to sustain. Two connectors reaching general availability this quarter move more of that burden into Eventstream. The Mirrored Database Change Feed connector consumes row-level inserts, updates, and deletes from change-feed-enabled mirrored databases. The MongoDB CDC connector supports MongoDB Atlas, cloud-hosted, and self-managed deployments. Both bring database changes into Eventstream's managed processing model, ready for the same DeltaFlow transformations available to other CDC sources. What shipped: Mirrored Database Change Feed connector (Generally Available), MongoDB CDC connector (Generally Available) Understand every event shape Streaming data rarely arrives in one consistent shape. A source may carry messages from multiple device types, application payloads may evolve, and teams may combine sources to improve utilization and reduce cost. Treating every payload as a union of every possible field makes exploration harder and creates long fragile transformations. Schema Registry and Event Schema Sets (Generally Available) provide reusable contracts for streaming data. Teams can define Avro schemas, group related schemas, retain earlier versions, compare changes, and discover schemas across Fabric workspaces. Schema-aware Eventstreams (Preview) lets one eventstream understand and process multiple event types. Events with registered schemas, along with change feeds from supported operational databases, are recognized automatically. For unschematized payloads, users can classify events with a field such as deviceType or entityType. A redesigned data preview makes it easier to inspect each event: Browse and inspect nested JSON structures View event headers and metadata along with the actual payload Download selected events Figure: Processing mixed events from schematized and un-schematized sources within a single schema-aware eventstream What shipped: Schema Registry and Event Schema Sets (Generally Available), Schema-aware Eventstreams (Preview). Add business context in flight Live events often contain only a device ID, customer ID, or product code. Without the surrounding business context, downstream systems cannot make an informed decision until a separate batch process enriches the data once it reaches an analytical store. Reference Data with Delta Table (Preview) brings that enrichment into Eventstream. A live event can join with reference data in a Lakehouse or warehouse table, including shortcut-backed Delta tables. No-code INNER and LEFT OUTER joins cover common patterns, while the SQL experience supports more complex logic. The event gains business meaning before it is routed, not after. Figure: Reference Data Join adds business context to an event before it's routed to a destination. What shipped: Reference Data with Delta table (Preview) Detect issues and act faster A streaming pipeline can appear to be running even when a node falls behind, events arrive outside the expected time window, or a destination rejects processed values. A top-level running state is not enough to diagnose these conditions. This quarter adds a more complete operating loop around each Eventstream. Workspace Monitoring helps teams observe throughput, backlog, watermark delay, errors, and node health. Processing logs and editor validation help diagnose malformed input, query failures, type-conversion errors, event-time policy violations, recovery events, and destination-access problems. Teams can act by creating and managing Activator rules without leaving Eventstream, then optimize capacity by routing Capacity Operation Events through Eventstream for operation-level analysis, alerting, and governance. What shipped: Workspace Monitoring for Eventstream (Preview), Workspace Monitoring diagnostic-log support (Preview), Activator rule management in Eventstream (Generally Available), Capacity Operation Events source (Preview). Secure and deploy eventstreams consistently Enterprise streaming workloads often need private connectivity, environment-specific configuration, and explicit control over where data can flow. Workspace-level Private Link (Preview) for Eventstream lets administrators apply private inbound connectivity to selected Fabric workspaces instead of imposing the same network posture across the tenant. Variable Library support (Preview) keeps environment-specific connections, item references, parameters, and value sets separate from pipeline logic. Teams can carry one Eventstream across development, test, and production without embedding each environment's values in the definition. These capabilities build on existing support for private and on-premises sources, workspace identity, custom certificate authorities, mutual TLS, and outbound access protection. What shipped: Workspace-level Private Link for Eventstream (Preview), Variable Library support for Eventstream (Preview). What this quarter adds up to Together, these updates create a more complete path from incoming events to business action. Teams can understand mixed payloads, enrich events while they are moving, bring in operational changes, connect managed or custom sources, diagnose processing problems, and carry the same Eventstream safely across environments. title: More expressive graph analysis: GQL improvements in Microsoft Fabric Graph
text: Coauthors: Idris Motiwala, and Justin Fine January–August 2026 updates expand how users find, inspect, compose, and analyze connections. Organizations use graph data to understand how information moves between systems, how services depend on one another, how conversations develop, and how people or organizations relate. Graph Query Language (GQL) in Microsoft Fabric Graph helps users explore and analyze those connections with standardized query patterns. From January through August 2026, new GQL capabilities made it easier to control traversals, inspect paths, compose multistage queries, summarize connected data, and work with complex values. These improvements help analysts express more graph questions in a single query and give developers finer control over query behavior. The following sections explain where each capability is useful and show the associated syntax. Find and control paths Shortest paths with ANY SHORTEST When several paths connect two entities, many applications need one shortest path rather than every possible path. ANY SHORTEST makes that intent explicit. This is useful for dependency analysis, recommendations, network routing, and investigations where fewer intermediate steps are preferred. MATCH ANY SHORTEST ({id: 1})->{,2}(d) RETURN d.id AS dst Quantified edge patterns Quantified edge patterns repeat a complete relationship pattern and can apply conditions to intermediate nodes. In the following example, each repeated step requires the source person to use Chrome. This gives developers more control than repeating only an edge pattern. MATCH p=(a:Person {id: 987})((x)-[k:knows]->() WHERE x.browserUsed = 'Chrome'){2}(b:Person) FOR n IN NODES(p) WITH OFFSET off RETURN n.browserUsed ORDER BY a.id, b.id, off LIMIT 12 Complete path modes Path modes define whether a traversal can revisit nodes or edges. WALK permits repetition. TRAIL prevents repeated edges. SIMPLE prevents repeated interior nodes. ACYCLIC prevents any repeated node. DIFFERENT EDGES prevent one edge from satisfying more than one edge variable in the match. These choices help query results reflect the meaning of a route, hierarchy, or dependency chain. MATCH WALK (:Person {firstName: "Juliana"})-[:studyAt]->(:University) MATCH TRAIL (:Person {firstName: "Juliana"})-[:studyAt]->(:University) MATCH SIMPLE (x)->{2}(y) RETURN COUNT(*) AS path_count MATCH ACYCLIC (x:`node` {id: 1})->(y)->(z) RETURN x.id, y.id, z.id ORDER BY x.id, y.id, z.id MATCH DIFFERENT EDGES (p:Person {name: 'Keanu Reeves'})-[e:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie) RETURN m.title AS movie Unbounded variable-length path patterns Variable-length paths previously required a maximum hop count. Unbounded quantifiers allow the graph structure to determine the traversal depth when no meaningful fixed limit exists. The example follows one or more relationships, while ACYCLIC prevents the traversal from visiting the same node twice. Unbounded refers to the path expression, not unlimited compute, so use selective starting points and test performance with representative graph density. MATCH ACYCLIC ()-[]->{1,}() RETURN COUNT(*) AS total Inspect paths and graph elements NODES, EDGES, and INNER_NODES These functions expose the contents of a matched path. NODES returns all nodes in the path, EDGES returns all relationships in the path, and INNER_NODES returns the intermediate nodes without the endpoints. Applications can use these results to explain lineage, dependencies, and investigative findings instead of returning only a destination. MATCH p=({id: 1})-[]->{0,4}(z) RETURN NODES(p) AS res_nodes, INNER_NODES(p) AS res_inner_nodes ORDER BY z.id ELEMENT_ID ELEMENT_ID returns the identity of a graph element. It is useful when an application must compare, track, or reference a specific node or edge independently of its business properties. MATCH (x) RETURN ELEMENT_ID(x) AS vid, x AS actual_id ORDER BY x.id LIMIT 5 SOURCE and DESTINATION SOURCE and DESTINATION identify the endpoints of an edge. This makes directional checks and edge-centric analysis easier, especially when a query starts from a relationship rather than a node. MATCH (x)-[e]->() RETURN x.id, SOURCE(e).id AS s ORDER BY e.src, e.dst LIMIT 10 MATCH ()-[e]->(x) RETURN false IN COLLECT_LIST(x = DESTINATION(e)) AS no Compose larger queries NEXT NEXT passes the output of one query stage into the next, allowing analysts to express a multistep question in a single query. For example, they can calculate a measure, filter the result, traverse another relationship, and summarize the final result without moving intermediate data into application code. MATCH (m:Message)-[:hasCreator]-(p:Person) RETURN p, AVG(m.length) AS avg_msg_length GROUP BY p NEXT FILTER avg_msg_length > 100u MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(:Person) RETURN avg_msg_length, COUNT(*) AS connections GROUP BY p, avg_msg_length EXISTS subqueries EXISTS answers a yes-no question about another graph pattern. It can filter rows or participate inside an aggregate without requiring the outer query to return the matching details. MATCH (x) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (y) WHERE y.id = 5 RETURN y } RETURN x.id AS xid ORDER BY xid MATCH (x) RETURN COUNT(*) FILTER ( WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (x)-[]->(y) RETURN y } ) AS count_with_out CALL subqueries CALL runs a contained query for each current outer result. In the example, it calculates each node’s outgoing degree and returns that value with the node identifier, keeping the intermediate calculation contained within the query. MATCH (x) CALL { MATCH (x)-[e]->(y) RETURN COUNT(e) AS out_degree } RETURN x.id AS xid, out_degree ORDER BY xid OPTIONAL CALL OPTIONAL CALL preserves the outer row when the contained query has no match. This supports enrichment scenarios where related information is useful but not required. MATCH (x {id: 1}) OPTIONAL CALL { MATCH (y)-[]->(x) RETURN y.id AS yid } RETURN x.id AS xid, yid ORDER BY yid UNION DISTINCT UNION DISTINCT combines compatible result sets and removes duplicate rows. It complements UNION ALL, which preserves duplicates, so the query can choose the correct set behavior. MATCH () LIMIT 3 RETURN 42 AS x UNION MATCH () LIMIT 3 RETURN 100u AS x Summarize connected data Filtered and paged aggregates Filtered aggregates calculate a summary over a selected subset. Paging controls such as LIMIT can be applied within the aggregate, giving developers precise control over which values contribute to the result. MATCH (m:Movie) RETURN COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE m.released Nested aggregations Nested aggregation supports layered questions, such as finding the minimum of averages calculated across groups or paths. This reduces the need to move intermediate results into application code. MATCH (a:`node`)-[e:`edge`]->{1,2}(b:`node`) RETURN a.id AS id, MIN(AVG(e.weight)) AS min_average GROUP BY id COLLECT_ONE, COLLECT_LIST, and COLLECT_ELEMENTS Collection functions retain values or graph elements for evaluation as a group. COLLECT_ONE selects one value, COLLECT_LIST builds a list, and COLLECT_ELEMENTS gathers graph elements. They are useful for path-level checks, ordered output, and analysis across repeated relationships. MATCH (p:`node` {id: 1})-[e]->{2}(p1:`node` {id: 1}) RETURN (COLLECT_ONE(e.weight) IN [e[0].weight, e[1].weight]) AS contained MATCH ()-[e]->{1,2}() RETURN COLLECT_LIST(ALL e.weight) AS w ORDER BY w LIMIT 20 MATCH ()-[a:ACTED_IN]->{0,4}() WHERE SIZE(COLLECT_ELEMENTS(DISTINCT a.roles)) > 4 RETURN TO_JSON_STRING(a.roles) AS r Work with values and text Dynamic nested data Support for dynamic nested data lets queries work with richer values that do not fit a flat property model. This is useful when graph entities contain structured application payloads, nested attributes, or evolving schemas. CAST CAST converts a value to a supported target type. Explicit conversion makes comparisons and calculations more predictable when source data contains different numeric types. RETURN CAST(42 AS DOUBLE) AS double_res, CAST(42 AS UINT) AS uint_res, CAST(42.5d AS INT) AS int_res R

title: T-SQL language enhancements in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview)
text: Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse is expanding its T-SQL capabilities with four language enhancements in preview. GROUP BY ALL, ORDER BY ALL, the QUALIFY clause, and the FROM ... SELECT query format help SQL developers and data professionals reduce repetitive code, simplify query maintenance, and make analytical logic easier to understand. Figure: A T-SQL query uses GROUP BY ALL and ORDER BY ALL in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse. What’s new Four T-SQL language enhancements are available in preview: GROUP BY ALL — automatically groups by every non-aggregate expression in the SELECT list, reducing duplication between SELECT and GROUP BY clauses. ORDER BY ALL — sorts results by each column in the SELECT list, using the same column order, so developers do not need to repeat every sort expression. QUALIFY — filters rows after window functions are evaluated, so common ranking and top-N patterns no longer require an additional subquery or common table expression. FROM ... SELECT — provides an alternative query format that begins with the data source and defines the selected columns later, allowing developers to write complex queries in a source-first sequence. These additions reduce repetitive code and make query intent easier to understand. They are especially valuable when queries include many grouping or sorting columns, when analytical results require filtering, or when a source-first structure makes complex logic easier to follow and maintain. Together, these enhancements make queries easier to adapt as requirements change. Developers can add or remove projected columns with less rework, filter analytical results without an extra query layer, and organize complex queries in the sequence that best matches how they reason about the data. New capabilities: Write shorter queries with less repeated code. Make grouping, ordering, and analytical filtering easier to understand. Reduce maintenance when projected columns change. Express source-first query logic in a clear, natural sequence. Use familiar T-SQL capabilities directly in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse. Conclusion These T-SQL language enhancements make everyday query development in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse more concise and expressive. Whether you are summarizing data, sorting wide result sets, filtering window-function results, or organizing complex query flows, the new syntax helps you focus on analytical intent instead of repetitive code. For syntax, supported options, and examples, refer to the documentation for QUALIFY , GROUP BY ALL , ORDER BY ALL , and FROM ... SELECT . As you evaluate these preview capabilities, share your scenarios and feedback with the Microsoft Fabric community on Reddit .

title: New analytical functions in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview)
text: Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint now support new analytical functions in preview. SQL developers and data professionals can calculate medians, quantiles, and percentiles with concise, maintainable T-SQL queries. What’s new in preview MEDIAN — returns the middle value in a dataset. QUANTILE — returns the value at a specified point in a distribution. APPROX_MEDIAN — estimates the median for large datasets. APPROX_QUANTILE — estimates a specified quantile for large datasets. PERCENTILE_CONT and PERCETILE_DISC — The existing PERCENTILE_CONT and PERCENTILE_DISC analytical functions now also support aggregate syntax, complementing their window forms for continuous and discrete percentile analysis. With these functions, you can calculate distribution metrics without writing multi-step workarounds. For example, you can compare a transaction with the median for its customer segment, identify quantile thresholds, summarize performance, and explore distributions across large datasets. The following query shows the four new functions and the enhanced aggregate syntax for PERCENTILE_CONT and PERCENTILE_DISC in a Fabric Data Warehouse T-SQL workload. Figure: A T-SQL query uses the new analytical functions to calculate distribution metrics in Fabric Data Warehouse. You can use each function as an aggregate to return one result for a dataset or group, or as a window function to add the analytical result to each row while preserving the result set. Why it matters These capabilities simplify common distribution analysis: Write shorter, easier-to-maintain analytical queries. Analyze data directly in the warehouse. Choose exact calculations when precision is the priority, or approximate calculations when you need faster results across large datasets. Use the same analytical patterns across Fabric Data Warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint. Conclusion The new functions make it easier to perform common distribution analysis directly in Fabric Data Warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint. You can choose exact calculations when precision is the priority or approximate calculations when faster results at scale are more important, then use aggregate or window syntax to fit the analysis. This reduces custom query logic and keeps statistical analysis close to the data. For syntax, supported options, and examples, refer to the Aggregate functions (Transact-SQL) documentation . As you evaluate the preview, share your scenarios and feedback in the Microsoft Fabric community on Reddit .

title: Fabric Data Warehouse integration with Fabric User Data Functions (Preview)
text: Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse now integrates with Fabric User Data Functions in preview, so you can extend T-SQL with custom Python logic without building separate applications or pipelines. Use the integration to send email or Teams messages, retrieve parameters and secrets from Fabric variable libraries or Azure Key Vault, and access data across OneLake. These capabilities are now available directly from T-SQL queries in your Warehouse. Figure: Calling a Fabric User Data Function from a T-SQL query in Fabric Data Warehouse. You can create T-SQL external functions in Fabric Data Warehouse that reference Python functions in a Fabric User Data Functions item. You can then invoke those functions from familiar statements such as SELECT, INSERT, and UPDATE. When an external function is called, Data Warehouse delegates its execution to the Fabric User Data Functions runtime. This integration enables scenarios such as: Calling Fabric or external APIs and sending email, Teams messages, or notifications. Reading Excel, XML, PDF, and other file formats through Python. Accessing data in OneLake and reading from or writing to Fabric databases, Azure Cosmos DB, and warehouses across workspaces. Retrieving secrets and configuration values from Azure Key Vault or Fabric variable libraries to parameterize custom logic. Encrypting, decrypting, or masking sensitive columns with custom Python logic and organization-managed keys. Enriching and validating data by geocoding addresses, verifying VAT or IBAN numbers, or scoring records with a machine learning model. Example: Use Python to classify IPv6 network events from T-SQL Classifying IPv6 events by network prefix can support security analysis, but the required parsing and binary arithmetic are complex in T-SQL. Python provides a purpose-built standard library for this task, allowing warehouses that store network and security telemetry to organize events into consistent network ranges for analysis. In this example, Python’s ipaddress function accepts an IPv6 address and prefix length and returns the corresponding network in CIDR notation. Persisting this value as an analytics column lets downstream queries group events into consistent network ranges without repeating calculation. import ipaddress import fabric.functions as fn udf = fn.UserDataFunctions() @udf.function() def getIpv6Network(address: str, prefixLength: int) -> str: interface = ipaddress.ip_interface(f"{address}/{prefixLength}") return str(interface.network) The published Python function is mapped to a T-SQL external function that accepts an IPv6 address and prefix length and returns the corresponding network prefix in CIDR notation. CREATE FUNCTION ipv6.get_network AS EXTERNAL FUNCTION utilities.getIpv6Network; You can then calculate and persist a /48 network prefix for each event: UPDATE dbo.NetworkEvents SET NetworkPrefix = ipv6.get_network(SourceIp, 48) WHERE NetworkPrefix IS NULL; Each call to ipv6.get_network delegates execution to the Fabric User Data Function runtime. After the result is stored in NetworkPrefix column, downstream queries can use it without recalculating the prefix. Conclusion Fabric User Data Functions let teams continue working in T-SQL while using Python to address scenarios that traditionally require separate applications or pipelines. Explore the preview and start extending your Fabric Data Warehouse solutions with custom logic today. You learn how to use the User Data Functions in Fabric Data Warehouse in the documentation. Try this feature during the preview and share your feedback with the Microsoft Fabric community on Reddit .

title: Retiring the Fabric data agent custom tool in Microsoft Foundry: move to Fabric IQ
text: In March 2025, we announced that agents in Microsoft Foundry could use Fabric data agents to answer questions about data in Microsoft Fabric. In the earlier integration, you connected to a data agent by adding it as a custom tool. For details, refer to Consume a data agent in Microsoft Foundry . What’s changing We are deprecating the earlier custom-connection integration. Starting 11/6, 2026, that integration will no longer be supported. If your Foundry agents use a Fabric data agent as a custom tool, you must migrate them before that date. The replacement integration (Preview) uses the Fabric IQ (OneLake Catalog) tool, which makes your data available to agents and applications. In the Foundry portal, you can use this tool to add a published Fabric data agent to a Foundry agent. For configuration steps, refer to Consume Fabric data agent from Microsoft Foundry via Fabric IQ . Capabilities with the new integration The replacement integration changes how you find and connect Fabric data agents: Select accessible published data agents from the catalog. In the Foundry portal, the OneLake Catalog shows the published data agents available to you by name, so the connection workflow does not require you to enter a workspace ID or an artifact ID. Connect more than one data agent. A Foundry agent can call multiple data agents, such as separate agents for sales data and customer support data. The earlier custom-connection integration only supported one Fabric data agent. Connect through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint. MCP is an open standard for how an agent calls a tool. Each selected Fabric data agent is presented to the Foundry agent as a tool through a MCP endpoint. Coming soon, when a data agent answers a question, its response will also include the query it used to generate the answer. What you need to do If any of your Foundry agents use a Fabric data agent as a custom tool, complete the following steps before 11/6/2026: In Microsoft Fabric, make sure to publish your Fabric data agent with a rich and detailed description. Open the agent in the Microsoft Foundry portal. In the Tools section, add the Fabric IQ (OneLake Catalog) tool, and then select your data agent from the catalog. Update the Foundry agent's instructions. Name each data agent and describe the types of questions it should handle. Remove the earlier custom tool and then save the Foundry agent. Test the Foundry agent with representative questions for each connected data agent. If you connect data agents in code, update your implementation to use the Fabric IQ tool. For samples in Python, C#, and JavaScript, refer to Connect agents to Microsoft Fabric with Fabric IQ . Guides to migrate from Fabric Data Agent to Fabric IQ tool Option 1: Migrate in Foundry Portal Navigate to Foundry Portal and open the Tools Catalog, select “Fabric IQ (OneLake Catalog)”. Figure: Select FabricIQ (OneLake Catalog) from the tools . In the OneLake catalog, filter by “Data agent” type. Figure: Filter by Data Agent in the OneLake Catalog and select data agent. Select any data agent you want to use, and you are ready to go. Provide instructions to your Foundry agent about how to use Fabric data agent. Figure: Add Fabric data agent to your Foundry agent and provide instructions . Option 2: Migrate in SDK/Rest API After you publish the Fabric data agent, open its Settings and go to the Model Context Protocol tab. This tab shows: Data agent MCP server name MCP server URL (copy this value; you can use in every client) Data agent MCP tool name MCP server tool description Figure: Navigate to data agent setting to find the MCP server URL. Once you get the data agent MCP server URL, proceed with the following steps: Step 1: Get an access token az account get-access-token --resource https://management.azure.com --query accessToken -o tsv Step 2: Create a Foundry connection to the Fabric data agent A connection stores the Fabric data agent endpoint and how to sign in to it. Your agent uses this connection to reach Fabric. Replace each value in angle brackets, then run the request: curl --request PUT \ --url 'https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/ /resourceGroups/ /providers/Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/ /projects/ /connections/ ?api-version=2025-04-01-preview' \ --header 'Authorization: Bearer ' \ --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data '{ "type": "Microsoft.MachineLearningServices/workspaces/connections", "properties": { "authType": "UserEntraToken", "group": "AzureAI", "category": "RemoteTool", "target": " ", "audience": "https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/.default", "isSharedToAll": true, "sharedUserList": [], "UseCustomConnector": false, "Credentials": { "ClientId": "fake" }, "metadata": { "ApiType": "Azure" } } }' Main field capabilities: Field Value What it means authType UserEntraToken The agent calls Fabric as the signed in user, with that user's Microsoft Entra token. category RemoteTool The connection points to a remote tool, in this case an MCP endpoint. target Your MCP endpoint The address of your Fabric data agent. audience https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/.default The token is issued for the Fabric API. isSharedToAll true Every user in the Foundry project can use the connection. Credentials.ClientId fake Keep this value as shown. The response includes an id field. This is the full resource ID of the connection. Save it for step 4. It looks like this: /subscriptions/ /resourceGroups/ /providers/Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/ /projects/ /connections/ Step 3: Install the Python packages pip install "azure-ai-projects>=2.2.0" azure-identity Step 4: Set the environment variables Variable Where to find it FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT The Overview page of your Foundry project. FOUNDRY_MODEL_NAME The deployment name of your model in your Foundry project. FABRIC_IQ_PROJECT_CONNECTION_ID The full connection resource ID from step 2. Use the full ID, not only the connection name. export FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT=" " export FOUNDRY_MODEL_NAME=" " export FABRIC_IQ_PROJECT_CONNECTION_ID=" " Step 5: Create an agent that uses the Fabric IQ tool and ask it a question This script creates a prompt agent with the Fabric IQ tool, sends it one question, prints the answer, and then deletes the agent. import os from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential from azure.ai.projects import AIProjectClient from azure.ai.projects.models import PromptAgentDefinition, FabricIQPreviewTool endpoint = os.environ["FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT"] with ( # Signs in with your Azure command line interface account (from az login). DefaultAzureCredential() as credential, AIProjectClient(endpoint=endpoint, credential=credential) as project_client, project_client.get_openai_client() as openai_client, ): # 1. Define the Fabric IQ tool. It uses the connection you created in step 2. fabric_iq_tool = FabricIQPreviewTool( project_connection_id=os.environ["FABRIC_IQ_PROJECT_CONNECTION_ID"], require_approval="never", # The agent calls the tool without asking you first. ) # 2. Create the agent with your model, its instructions, and the Fabric IQ tool. agent = project_client.agents.create_version( agent_name="MyAgent", definition=PromptAgentDefinition( model=os.environ["FOUNDRY_MODEL_NAME"], instructions="Use the available Fabric IQ tools to answer questions and perform tasks.", tools=[fabric_iq_tool], ), ) print(f"Agent created (id: {agent.id}, name: {agent.name}, version: {agent.version})") # 3. Ask the agent a question. Change this to a question about your own data. user_input = "Which customers placed orders above $10,000 last quarter?" response = openai_client.responses.create( input=user_input, extra_body={"agent_reference": {"name": agent.name, "type": "agent_reference"}}, ) print(f"Agent response: {response.output_text}") # 4. Delete this agent version so unused versions don't build up in your project. project_client.agents.delete_version(agent_name=agent.name, agent_version=agent.version) print("Agent deleted") Finally, run

title: Advanced NL2SQL and advanced DAX generation in Fabric data agents (Generally Available)
text: Data agents in Microsoft Fabric let users ask questions about data in plain language. As a creator, you connect an agent to supported sources—including SQL databases, lakehouses, Power BI semantic models, and eventhouses—add the business context it needs, and share it with users across Fabric, Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, and Microsoft Foundry. The data agent can then respond like a domain expert that understands what your tables mean, how your metrics are defined, and which source can answer a question. The usefulness of a data agent ultimately depends on a simple question: can it translate what a user asks into the right query? That is harder than it sounds. Enterprise schemas are rarely intuitive. Several tables, columns, measures, or join paths may appear to answer the same question, so a query can be technically valid but still return the wrong result. Advanced NL2SQL and advanced DAX generation help address this problem by allowing the agent to explore the schema and data, validate assumptions, and refine its approach before generating a query. Both capabilities are available today, and we'll begin rolling the core improvements out to the standard runtime on November 2, with the rollout expected to complete by November 10. In this post, we'll look at how they work, what our internal benchmarks show, the new configurations available for shaping how the agent behaves, and what to consider as you re-test and evaluate your data agents. Why conversational analytics gets harder with enterprise data Turning a plain-language question into a correct query is a complicated problem, both for SQL and DAX, requiring the agent to resolve several challenges at once: Schemas are large. Enterprise sources can contain hundreds of tables, columns, and measures, and the names alone may not explain when or how they should be used. Business context exists outside the data. Definitions such as “revenue” or “active customer” often live in documentation, previous queries, or analysts’ knowledge rather than in the source schema. Filter values must match the way data is stored. Users describe concepts naturally, but those concepts must map to the values in the data. For example, a user may ask about “California” when the relevant column stores the value “CA.” Questions are ambiguous. More than one column, calculation, or join may appear to satisfy a request. Individually, each of these can be managed with enough hand-written guidance. The difficulty is that they compound: a single-pass generator has to resolve all of them at once — your schema, your definitions, your filter values — committing to an interpretation before it has any evidence that interpretation is right. When it guesses wrong, the query still runs, and the answer looks no different from a correct one. Advanced NL2SQL and advanced DAX generation are built around that problem. Rather than generating a single pass, the agent gathers evidence first. Advanced NL2SQL: the agent explores before it writes The shift is architectural. Instead of one-shot generation, the agent has sub-tools to explore schema, test joins, and look up real filter values before it writes SQL. Under the hood, you can inspect each step the agent took, and the assumptions and reasoning behind it. It operates in three modes, each backed by its own sub-tools: Mode What it does Example query following Finds a relevant example query and answers by making approved modifications, such as literal filter or parameter substitutions. Clarifying questions Determines it can’t answer reliably without more information and asks targeted clarifying questions before generating SQL. Data exploration When no example directly applies, learns from existing example queries to infer business logic, explores the data to validate assumptions, and iteratively refines its approach. What you get as a creator: Advanced NL2SQL explores the SQL source schema, tests joins, and looks up real filter values before generating SQL, helping it choose the appropriate tables, columns, relationships, and filters. Schema descriptions and topics that teach the agent what your data means, so you get better answers with fewer instructions. Better example-following and filter-value substitution for novel questions. Handles large schemas far better and runs faster end to end, with more reasoning detail for debugging. New configurations: schema descriptions and topics Two new configurations give the agent more of the context it needs. Both are available for SQL data sources on the preview runtime. Schema descriptions Schema descriptions attach business context to the objects in your data source — what a table holds, what a column represents, and how each should be used. The agent uses them to interpret large or ambiguous schemas and generate a more accurate query. They matter most where object names don’t carry meaning on their own, or where several tables and columns look interchangeable. Figure: Schema descriptions add business context to schema objects, helping the data agent interpret your data. Topics Topics help you give the agent detailed guidance without sending every instruction with every question. The agent searches your topic content and uses only the sections relevant to the current request. Use data source instructions for rules that must always apply, and use topics for deeper guidance that applies only to a specific subject. You can write topics in Markdown, import multiple files, and review the run steps to see which topics the agent selected.
